idiom_name: Model.findAll / prisma.user.findMany as the collection-like interface
implementation_notes: Node has no persistence primitives beyond the driver, so the dominant ORMs supply the collection-like surface: User.findAll({ where }) (Sequelize) or prisma.user.findMany({ where }) (Prisma) return domain objects and hide SQL, while transactions come from the ORM (sequelize.transaction, Prisma interactive transactions). In JavaScript the pragmatic repository is a module of functions over that surface; a repository class is worth adding only when the domain must not import the ORM or when an in-memory implementation is needed for tests.
pitfalls: Returning ORM model instances past the module boundary leaks lazy-loaded associations and transaction objects into callers; map to plain objects when the boundary matters.
Without a managed transaction object, concurrent async calls interleave between read and write, so read-modify-write silently loses updates; use sequelize.transaction or prisma.$transaction.
A Knex/Objection-style query builder exposed through the repository is not a repository: callers end up writing the queries, which is exactly what the pattern exists to prevent.

variants.name: ORM model query API used directly as the repository surface

variants.name: Hand-written repository module over the ORM
variants.idiom_name: ES module exporting domain-language functions, ORM kept private
variants.implementation_notes: The classic form in JavaScript is a module (or factory) per aggregate that exports domain-language functions and imports the ORM privately, so callers never see models, options objects or SQL; tests substitute the module or inject a fake client. Choose it for hexagonal or DDD-style Node services where the domain layer must stay free of ORM imports, and when the same interface needs an in-memory implementation for fast tests.
pitfalls: A factory returning fresh closures per call is fine, but a module-level singleton client makes test isolation impossible; inject the client instead.
The mapping functions (toInvoice/toRow) are where drift happens: keep then in one module and cover them with round-trip tests.
Because nothing enforces the boundary, an import of the ORM inside domain files creeps in; add a lint rule on the domain folder if the separation matters.
